title: Trump's War in Iran in spotlight ahead of midterms
description: After President Trump slapped down reports that he is considered renewed strikes against Iran ahead of the midterms, the politics of the war he
body:
After President Trump slapped down reports that he is considered renewed strikes against Iran ahead of the midterms, the politics of the war he started are in the spotlight.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:  President Trump made an announcement about the war in Iran on social media.MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:  He explicitly linked the unpopular war to the midterm elections. And this is a quote. "We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on November 3." Unquote. OK, why do that? Apparently, to refute reports that the White House is considering airstrikes against Iran before Election Day.INSKEEP: OK. So the president is making this explicit connection between his decisions on a war involving the United States and his political fortunes at home. So let's bring in an expert on politics, NPR senior political editor and correspondent Domenico Montanaro. Good morning.DOMENICO MONTANARO, BYLINE: Hey there, Steve.INSKEEP: OK, what is notable about this post?MONTANARO: I mean, it's a little surprising that any president at war would want to tip their hand in either direction and make any kind of declarative promise pledging not to strike. You know, if we asked at the Pentagon or White House - are you going to strike before the election? - we'd be chided for asking such a silly question because...INSKEEP: Yes.MONTANARO: ...They're not going to tell us in the media, right? But Trump doing this is a very clear sign that he knows this war has been bad for his party politically ahead of these midterms. The reality is more strikes and further engagement, it's a tough sell for an American audience, including for many in Trump's base. I mean, Trump explicitly promised to not get into foreign entanglements.He even said in his inaugural that his presidency might be measured by the wars he didn't get into. You know, prolonged unpopular wars, we know, can be and have been dangerous for any president and his party. Think about Iraq, Vietnam, Korea. And all of that's heightened even more in October of an election year when the president's already unpopular, the cost of living and gas prices are putting Republicans on their back foot across the country.INSKEEP: Yeah, so I'm thinking this through. The president says don't worry about the war. I'm not going to remind you about the war until you vote for my party, and then maybe I'll resume the war after I get your vote. I mean, that seems to be the message here. But I was just out interviewing voters in the last few days, Domenico. They seem to be aware that there is a war on.MONTANARO: You know, this war is very unpopular if you look at public opinion. A recent AP-NORC poll, for example, found that 7 in 10 disapprove of how Trump is handling the war. And they say the war has not been worth fighting. Trump argues that it is worth it because he doesn't want Iran to have a nuclear weapon, though his rationale for this war certainly shifted quite a bit from the beginning of it. And it's hard to believe that this has been going on since February, much longer than promised. And historically in this country, wars that have dragged on have become major political problems for presidents.INSKEEP: I guess we should note also the president has said he is thinking the Iranians will be willing to settle with him after the midterms. So maybe he's hoping not to have to strike at all. But doesn't he face a historic problem here in terms of the popularity of this thing?MONTANARO: Yeah, he is. I mean, you know, I wrote about this back in March a few weeks after the war in Iran started, right after Trump had declared, quote, "we won." Back then, there had been no real rally around the flag effect, as it's known in polling when the country unifies and a president benefits, like when a country's attacked and the country feels compelled to respond. But this was a war of choice. And Americans have been war-weary from decades in Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria.When all this started, Trump's approval rating was sitting at 48% in an average of the polls. Now it's down to 37%. You know, it's a similar drop to what we saw, frankly, for President Biden after the chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan. And he never really recovered, especially as he was also dealing with a difficult economy.INSKEEP: So what does this mean for the elections that are underway in some places?MONTANARO: Yeah, it's not great for Trump and the Republican Party. That's why you've seen several Republicans distancing themselves from the war and the president's policies in recent weeks. Most Republicans I talk to can see that they're probably going to lose the House majority. And they're trying to hang onto a majority in the Senate, having to be on defense in a lot of red states, which they never thought would be the case when this cycle started.INSKEEP: It's just amazing to think about an election that could be decided in Kansas or Iowa or Texas.MONTANARO: Exactly.INSKEEP: Domenico, thanks so much.MONTANARO: You're welcome.INSKEEP: That's NPR's Domenico Montanaro.

title: 25 years later an Afghan couple looks back at the invasion
description: 25 years later an Afghan couple looks back at the invasion   Twenty-five years ago this week, the U.S. invaded Afghanistan. For StoryCorps, one Afghan
body:
25 years later an Afghan couple looks back at the invasion   Twenty-five years ago this week, the U.S. invaded Afghanistan. For StoryCorps, one Afghan couple offers an account of their experience after the invasion and eventual U.S. withdrawal.

   
    
        
            
            
            
        


    
        NPR
    



      
                  
            October 9, 20264:24 AM ET
         
      
   
                              By                
            


      
      25 years later an Afghan couple looks back at the invasion 
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5989180/nx-s1-9958006" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    




      Twenty-five years ago this week, the U.S. invaded Afghanistan. For StoryCorps, one Afghan couple offers an account of their experience after the invasion and eventual U.S. withdrawal.   


    
        
          Transcript
        
    (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:  It's time now for StoryCorps and a remembrance of the U.S. war in Afghanistan that began 25 years ago. Captain Ahmad Khalid Noori was an Afghan special operations officer fighting alongside U.S. troops. Wida Saber worked in Afghanistan's presidential palace. One night, Noori showed up unexpectedly at Saber's home to ask for her hand in marriage.AHMAD KHALID NOORI: In our culture, it's very common for families to receive the proposed before marriage and to either accept or deny.WIDA SABER: And my mom said no to you. My father served in the military, and I lost my dad when I was 13 years old. My mom, she's thinking, my daughter will become a widow because this man working with the Afghan special forces.NOORI: And I kept asking again and again.SABER: And my mom said no to you.NOORI: But then Afghanistan collapsed.SABER: I remember you called my mom, and you said, I want to marry Wida tomorrow because we work with the government. If the Taliban find us, definitely, they will kill us.NOORI: Yes.SABER: And we organized the marriage for the next evening. I did not remember nothing, only that I said, yes, yes, yes, yes. And after that, we become a husband and wife. And the next day, you said, Wida, we should go to the airport. We only had one bag with our phone, passport and documents. I remember every Taliban checkpoints as much as I can, I try to cover my face by burqa, and I was so worried if Taliban capture you. We were lucky to escape that.NOORI: The very first day, when we got here in the United States, I remember I was really broken. Losing my country was the very saddest event of my life.SABER: Yes. I remember those tough days. But, luckily, during this new life, we blessed with a daughter, and she makes my heart, my mind, my soul very calm.NOORI: Yes. When I have a tough day and I get back home and I see her with two teeth smiling, that helped me to forget what was hard. She's our cause now. I feel very proud as a man, a husband, now as a dad. And the reason why I am resilient today, why I continue to move forward and not give up, it's because of you.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)MARTIN: Ahmad Khalid Noori and Wida Saber. They live in Virginia with their 3-year-old daughter. Their interview is archived at the Library of Congress.

title: Why mailing a ballot close to Election Day may get it rejected for a late postmark
description: A Wake County Board of Elections employe
body:
A Wake County Board of Elections employee prepares a mail-in ballot to be sent out to a voter in September in Raleigh, N.C.
                
                    Matt Ramey/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Matt Ramey/AP
    

   
   Relying on the U.S. Postal Service to return a mail-in ballot close to Election Day now comes with an additional risk for many voters — a late postmark that gets a vote rejected.   The risk stems from mailing system changes that began last year. And those changes have pushed some election officials to encourage voters to consider returning their ballots at their local election office or any available drop boxes instead.   The calls to avoid mailboxes also come as trust in the Postal Service delivering mail ballots on time has fallen, and after President Trump pushed to restrict voting by mail for the midterm elections but was blocked by the Supreme Court.   
   Election officials often use the date of the postmark that USPS stamps on envelopes to determine whether a ballot was sent by Election Day.   About a week before next month's Election Day, USPS says it plans to roll out special postmarking procedures at post offices affected by the changes as part of its "extraordinary measures" policy to boost mail service for federal general elections.   Still, the agency continues to recommend that voters mail back ballots at least a week before their state's deadline. And in states with a grace period for receiving late-arriving mail ballots, USPS recommends stopping by a post office to ask for a manual postmark to make sure a ballot gets postmarked on the same day it's mailed.   How mailing system changes led to the risk of late postmarks   Since April 2025, USPS has been rolling out cuts to daily mail pick-ups and processing changes at certain post offices, especially in rural areas. What USPS calls its "Regional Transportation Optimization" effort is part of a 10-year reorganization plan the agency began in 2021 to try to stabilize its finances.   As a result, USPS may not automatically stamp a date on an envelope the same day it's collected by a letter carrier or dropped off at a post office or a big blue collection box.   
   As part of its "extraordinary measures" for these midterms, USPS has instructed post offices affected by RTO to separate returned ballots from other mail starting Oct. 26 so that managers can manually add postmarks the day the ballots are collected.   
   That procedure was not in place during this year's primary elections, which saw increased ballot rejection rates in multiple states.   Elena Patel, a senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution, says she is encouraged by the steps USPS plans to take in the coming weeks to address concerns about late postmarks.   But the situation is still risky for voters, Patel adds, given that it's not clear how post offices will carry out these directives for the first time, particularly in places where staffing may be stretched.   For the general election, an additional 43,000 to 55,000 ballots around the country could be rejected for arriving late because of the RTO effort, according to a new analysis by Patel, who produced the estimates before USPS announced its final extraordinary measures policy.   "These are some of the realities of running a very large postal network on tight finances," says Patel, who once worked as an economist at the Postal Regulatory Commission.   USPS plans to take other "extraordinary measures" for mail-in ballots   USPS has outlined other extraordinary measures:   Starting Oct. 24, 10 days before Election Day, some post offices may extend their opening and closing times by a half-hour and set up lines or drive-through lanes just for voters who want to get a manual postmark for their mail-in ballot. And starting Oct. 26, USPS says it plans to speed up delivery of ballots.   Asked why it is not starting extraordinary measures 15 days before Election Day, as it did for the 2024 and 2022 elections, USPS said in a statement: "The time period for extraordinary measures is carefully considered in advance of each General Election, and it is based on a number of internal factors. The Postal Service has successfully delivered America's election mail for more than 150 years, and we are confident that we will do so again this year."   
   Still, some eligible voters who rely on voting by mail are between "a rock and a hard place" when trying to navigate the mailing system, says Michelle Sparck, director of Get Out the Native Vote, a voter education organization in Alaska.   No post offices in the state are affected by the RTO effort, but Sparck, a member of the Qissunamiut Tribe of Chevak, says she has come across many absentee voters in Alaska Native villages who had their ballots rejected — an outcome that she fears will discourage some from trying to vote again.   "The No. 1 reason for that was postmarking delays. Now, even on a good Alaskan day with no weather challenges, it doesn't mean we're going to have an operational post office on a business day during business hours," Sparck says. "It's always, always easier said than done to kind of go along with the system's rules. But the system doesn't exactly work for us."   For now, Sparck is encouraging eligible voters to make a plan to be an October voter and not wait until November's Election Day if they can.   "If there is an early voting opportunity in a community," Sparck says, "we're asking people to drop their ballots off with those folks so that it becomes part of the chain of custody."   Edited by Benjamin Swasey

title: How 'Musk' director Alex Gibney became a critic
description: Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk gestures
body:
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk gestures on stage at the Capital One Arena after President-elect Donald Trump is sworn in as the 47th President of the United States in Washington, DC on Monday, January 20, 2025.
                
                    Ken Cedeno/UPI/Alamy Live News
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Ken Cedeno/UPI/Alamy Live News
    

   
   Some time ago, Alex Gibney got curious about how Elon Musk accumulated impossibly vast amounts of wealth and power.   So the Oscar-winning documentarian did what he does best, spending four years of deep research into Musk's world to create a film that's nearly as many hours long, each minute kept riveting by a trove of dreadful facts, videos, legal documents and interviews with people close to the tech entrepreneur.   "I started out as — if not an admirer — at least somebody who is sort of interested in what he was doing and liked it," Gibney told Morning Edition host Steve Inskeep.    
   Gibney, who narrates the film, says he was a "proud" owner of a Tesla Powerwall energy storage system at his home and Tesla solar panels on his roof.    But Gibney's perspective shifted as he prepared his film, Musk, which opens in theaters Friday. It's due to stream on HBO in a few months.   "I became increasingly resentful and angry. When [Defense Secretary] Pete Hegseth basically said that they were now going to use xAI to be fully integrated into the Department of War, it was like an out-of-body experience," he said, referring to the artificial intelligence company founded by Musk that's behind the Grok AI assistant.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Alex Gibney spent four years making his nearly four-hour film Musk.
                
                    Jigsaw Productions
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jigsaw Productions
    

   
   Lawsuit threat   The leadup to the film's release has seen some controversy after Musk used several insults to describe Gibney — "an idiot" was among the mildest ones — and threatened a defamation lawsuit.   
   In a letter sent to Gibney's Jigsaw Productions company that emerged in September, Musk attorney Alex Spiro focused on an exchange between Gibney and Ashley St. Clair, a one-time MAGA influencer who had a child with the billionaire.   St. Clair describes in the film text messages Musk sent her before the November 2024 presidential election in which he said he was "feeling more optimistic" about Donald Trump winning because "tomorrow we unleash the anomaly in the matrix."    Musk further told St. Clair that he planned on tapping "'lasers' from space," adding that "I have over 10 thousand lasers in space right now."   
   In the film, Gibney asks St. Clair if she believes Musk's texts referred to satellites owned by his rocket company, SpaceX. She responds, "I don't know where else he has lasers."   NPR has obtained and authenticated the texts between Musk and St. Clair, which were sent on Oct. 6, 2024.     Spiro's letter, which NPR has also reviewed, says that Gibney made a "false" insinuation that SpaceX's Starlink satellites somehow uploaded votes for Trump in swing states, a debunked conspiracy theory.   "We don't claim that he changed votes in the 2024 election. All we do is to show that he was bragging to his lover that he had special access to understanding the outcome of the election in a way that other people didn't," Gibney told NPR. "Was he lying to her or was he just bragging or was he telling us something that we shouldn't know? I don't know. That's for the viewer to decide."   
   Gibney, who's previously investigated the likes of Enron and blood-testing startup executive Elizabeth Holmes in his films, said that when he trained his lens on Musk, he prepared for the possibility that the maverick CEO would try to sue him.   "We had a battery of lawyers reviewing everything that we did. I actually hired an independent fact checker to check our own fact checkers inside. So against the richest man, the truth is not always a defense, but I'm counting on his commitment to the principles of being a free speech absolutist."   Gibney also noted that a lawsuit would  trigger a discovery process by which he could subpoena Musk's internal documents.   

    
        
    
        
                    YouTube
                
        
   Overselling products?   As he took a closer look at SpaceX and Tesla, Gibney noticed that while the two companies "had achieved great things technologically... their stock price was way out of proportion to their actual economic value." The filmmaker says Musk achieved this by overselling his products.   SpaceX performed a vital service, ferrying equipment into space and developing rockets that could be reused cheaply.   But the film says Musk cast the company as an even grander venture, forever about to colonize Mars.   
   Tesla made popular electric cars, but the film says Musk oversold them as self-driving.   According to the film, they weren't made with enough sensors for that, which is why some have crashed. "That's a level of overpromising that leans into fraud," Gibney said.   NPR has reached out to Spiro, Musk's attorney, about the specific claims made in the film but has not heard back.   The broadcast version of this story was produced by Kaity Kline.

title: As crypto and prediction markets expand, their regulator shrinks
description: President Donald Trump shakes hands with
body:
President Donald Trump shakes hands with Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chairman Michael Selig during a meeting with technology leaders in the Roosevelt Room of the White House, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, in Washington.
                
                    Jacquelyn Martin/Associated Press
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jacquelyn Martin/Associated Press
    

   
   Trump-era staff reductions have significantly hampered enforcement at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and its ability to regulate burgeoning new prediction and cryptocurrency markets, where hundreds of billions are traded each week.   By the end of 2025, the CFTC had 21% fewer staff on its payroll when compared to the previous 10-year average, according to U.S. Office of Personnel Management data. Between January 2024 and January 2025 alone, staffing dropped 22%. And the number of CFTC enforcement actions dropped even further. The agency made nearly 80% fewer enforcement actions in 2025 when compared to the annual average for the previous decade, according to the agency's annual reports.   
   The CFTC started hemorrhaging staff soon after President Trump won the 2024 election. This was not a coincidence, according to Jeff Le Riche, who worked as a CFTC enforcement lawyer between 2005 and 2025.   "The Trump administration had run partially on a platform that it would be friendlier to the crypto industry," Le Riche said.   Leading up to the 2024 election, the CFTC under the Biden administration had leveled enforcement cases against cryptocurrency companies such as Gemini, Mirror Trading, Voyager, Celsius and FTX for fraud. It did the same against the crypto prediction market Polymarket.   After President Trump's inauguration, "in order to show results to that industry, some people were punished for bringing those cases," Le Riche continued. "The end result was that a lot of the people that worked on those cases either left or were forced out."   
   In a statement to NPR, the CFTC did not address that claim directly, but praised the work of current agency head Michael Selig.   "The CFTC remains committed to promoting integrity and responsible innovation in U.S. derivatives markets, and Chairman Selig is grateful to the dedicated staff who continue to support this mission each day," CFTC spokesman Zach Fulton wrote in part.   
   To Le Riche, the 21% drop in employees and the nearly 80% decline in enforcement action go hand in hand.   "It castrated the enforcement team," Le Riche said. "Many of the people who were targeted were high-performing attorneys who had brought some of the most consequential and complicated cases over the past few years."   Joe Konizeski, who worked as a CFTC enforcement lawyer for 26 years, was one of the dozens forced out in 2025.   
   "The acting chair [Caroline Pham] said, 'We're closing all our crypto [cases],'" Konizeski said. "And so, of course, everybody who had a crypto scam had to close it and any matter that was even marginally related to crypto ended up getting closed."   Pham left the CFTC in December of 2025 and is now the chief legal and administrative officer at MoonPay, a cryptocurrency company. She did not respond to NPR's request for comment about whether she gave preferential treatment to the crypto industry.   Since Trump took office, the CFTC has rolled back its enforcement actions against crypto firms Gemini, Celsius, and FTX. But crypto cases weren't the only ones impacted. Konizeski said decreased staffing caused the CFTC to dismiss others such as a foreign exchange fraud case against WorldWideMarkets Inc. The company was accused of defrauding millions from users.   
   Before the explosion of the crypto and prediction markets, the CFTC largely focused on more traditional derivative markets — such as grain and stock futures contracts.   "Fewer cops on the beat… creates a real incentive to start engaging in fraudulent and deceitful behavior," Konizeski said. "Enforcement is down and that means that there's going to be more fraud."   
   For Konizeski, chief examples of this are prediction market advertisements that target young men. He accused Polymarket and Kalshi of "using fraudulent means" to entice young men to its platforms.   "CFTC knows this and allows it to continue," Konizeski said.   Neither Polymarket nor Kalshi responded to NPR's requests for comment about whether their advertising targeted young men.   A former CFTC lawyer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of professional repercussions, said they left the agency voluntarily soon after Trump took office and Pham curbed enforcement.   "Enforcement was particularly closed in crypto and prediction market cases," this former CFTC staffer said. "A lot of people left because, once Pham took over, it became clear that enforcement was not a priority."   Federal probe investigates CFTC staffing    The Government Accountability Office, a congressional watchdog agency, is now investigating the CFTC for its workforce reduction, according to a letter obtained by NPR. This new GAO probe into the CFTC comes after Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., requested a federal investigation into the agency's staffing and fraud enforcement in July.   "It's supposed to be out there regulating the market, but it doesn't appear to be doing it and frankly, doesn't appear to have the people to do it," Warren told NPR in an interview. "I want to know whether or not the watchdog is actually out there doing a little barking, or has the watchdog been locked up somewhere back in the barn?"   The GAO is gathering staff and resources for its investigation into the CFTC and will "initiate" the probe in December.   
   The CFTC did not directly comment on the GAO investigation but did respond to NPR's questions about its staffing levels.   "[The CFTC] is on track to hire roughly 100 employees in mission critical areas by the end of 2026," wrote CFTC spokesman Fulton in a statement. "Like many federal agencies, a number of CFTC staff opted to step away from public service in recent years, and the CFTC will continue to ensure it attracts and retains talented staff dedicated to fulfilling our critical mission."   During 2026, the CFTC has seen a slight uptick in staffing.   While the GAO investigation is narrowly focused on staff reduction, Warren said Congress could use its "power to investigate" possible corruption citing potential Congressional subpoenas and its ability to control the agency's funding.   "But that only happens if Congress has the backbone and right now, led by the Republicans, Congress not only doesn't have a backbone, it doesn't even have any interest in doing it," Warren said.   When asked if a Democratic Congress would subpoena the heads of the CFTC, crypto companies and prediction markets, Warren said, "it is our job to use all those tools to investigate."   Crypto at the White House    In August, the current chair of the CFTC, Michael Selig, celebrated his agency's slowdown in enforcement actions during a White House event featuring the crypto industry.   "The era of political lawfare, debanking and regulation by enforcement is over," Selig said while flanked by crypto CEOs in the Roosevelt Room. "Innovators, like the people in this room, are welcome to the White House — not railroaded to the big house."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Coinbase CEO and co-founder Brian Armstrong speaks as President Donald Trump meets with technology leaders in the Roosevelt Room of the White House, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, in Washington.
                
                    Jacquelyn Martin/Associated Press
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jacquelyn Martin/Associated Press
    

   
   He argued that the U.S. needs to "dominate" these new financial technologies — like crypto and prediction markets — and "write the rules that define the next generation of financial markets." Selig is the sole member of the normally five-member CFTC commission, giving him unchallenged power over the direction of the agency.   
   Before his time at the CFTC, Selig was a corporate lawyer for cryptocurrency firms and prediction markets. His latest financial disclosure report shows that Selig sold between $65,000 and $150,000 in Bitcoin before he became a commissioner.   While Selig wants increased agency rule making for prediction and crypto markets, that requires a massive amount of work and staffing, according to former CFTC director Brian Young, who said the reduction in headcount limits the agency's ability to write new rules.   "With the growth of prediction markets and digital asset trading, the [CFTC] really needs to augment staffing in order to meet these increased responsibilities," Young said. "At the end of the day, they need people to process these applications."   A former CFTC employee — who speaks regularly with current employees — told NPR that the CFTC is so understaffed that it is struggling to execute Trump's 2025 executive order on cryptocurrency.   "My friends that are there are dying," this former staffer told NPR on the condition of anonymity for fear of professional retaliation.   Earlier this year, CFTC Inspector General Christopher Skinner acknowledged the difficulty of short staffing in a recent annual report.   "The CFTC should consider human capital management as a top priority," Skinner wrote. "To ensure the agency has the appropriate talent and skill sets to meet an expanding regulatory landscape."   Meanwhile, the CFTC's work load keeps growing.   In 2025, the agency greenlit six prediction markets — three times the average annual rate over the last decade. This year, the agency has authorized another 6 prediction markets with 18 applications pending.   After the Senate failed to advance a major crypto and banking regulation bill this summer, the CFTC announced this week that it is moving ahead with making its own rules without congressional input.   "The American people deserve clarity, certainty, and consumer protections in the crypto asset markets and the agency is committed to delivering this by incorporating crypto asset transactions into its uniform national market regulatory framework," Selig said in a statement.   
   Still, as of July, the agency's workforce was 16% below its decade-average or 100 staffers short. The CFTC is currently hiring for seven full-time positions.

title: Toss-ups, triage and targets: How to read the wide-open 2026 House map
description: A general view of voting machines at the
body:
A general view of voting machines at the Franklin County Board of Elections on Oct. 6, 2026 in Columbus, Ohio.
                
                    Jeff Dean/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jeff Dean/Getty Images
    

   
   Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly.      With just under a month to go until Election Day, financial decisions made by both parties appear to suggest the question being asked is not if Democrats take control of the House, but how large the majority may be.   Currently, Republicans hold a narrow 218-214 seat advantage. In February 2025, the Cook Political Report's initial ratings for the midterms found a small slice of 39 races listed as competitive, with 18 classified as "toss-ups."   That topline number has shifted, with Cook currently listing 43 districts as competitive, including 22 toss-ups. But beyond that, under the hood, Democratic and Republican groups are marshalling hundreds of millions of dollars to influence an electoral landscape that is much larger.   
   An NPR analysis of both parties' campaign targets, future ad reservations and outside spending by Trump-aligned super PACs finds more than 90 districts where resources are being committed in the closing weeks of the midterms.   Here's a look at the types of races that will decide who controls the House in 2027.   
   Competitive races on paper   If the political environment remained unchanged from the 2024 presidential election, a small group of House races would be competitive no matter what, like the 10 districts that voted for one party's presidential candidate and the other party's House nominee. (Not counting those changed by redistricting in the last 18 months, but more on that below.)   That includes the seats held by New York Republican Rep. Mike Lawler (NY-17), Pennsylvania Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-01) and Washington state Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (WA-03). Another group of seats had very close margins in 2024, like Democratic Rep. Adam Gray's victory by fewer than 200 votes in California's 13th Congressional District and a 799-vote victory for Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa's 1st Congressional District.   
   But this is not the same political environment as 2024. President Trump's unpopularity with voters has reached record highs, with the share of voters who strongly disapprove of his job performance sitting higher than any point in either term in office.   Voters are unhappy with the ongoing war in Iran, rising gas prices, tariffs and immigration enforcement, and a wave of anti-incumbent sentiment has driven a record number of congressional retirement announcements along with a number of sitting lawmakers losing their primary races this year.   
   Other races to watch: CO-08, NY-03, PA-08, PA-10    Redistricting    Further scrambling the map: a redistricting arms race that resulted in new district lines for an estimated 1 in 10 registered voters across several states.   Republican-led state legislatures, at Trump's urging and in some cases threats, tried to draw new House maps that would give them multiple additional seats in states like Texas and Florida, while Democrats countered in California.   But many of the new district lines were drawn with assumptions made about voters who backed President Trump in 2024 and what they would do in 2026, and in some cases, could backfire.   
   According to Strength in Numbers/Verasight polling data shared with NPR, Trump has lower-than-average job approval in communities that make up newly redrawn districts in South Florida and along the Texas-Mexico border, like TX-28 and FL-25.   In North Carolina's 1st Congressional District, Democrat Rep. Don Davis saw his district that Trump narrowly carried in 2024 become even more conservative. But the national environment — and a U.S. Senate race where polls show Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper leading — has made the contest more competitive. More than $20 million in ad reservations are scheduled between now and Election Day in the rural and coastal district, making it one of the most expensive House races in the country.   Other races to watch: AL-02, OH-09, FL-22, TX-35   Following the money and messaging   Heading into the final electoral sprint, there are 60 districts that are listed as priorities of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the National Republican Congressional Committee along with Trump-aligned super PACs like No Going Back.   On average, those districts voted for Trump by an 8% margin in 2024, highlighting how deep into conservative areas competitive races have moved.   The DCCC has more than 90 districts on its battlefield map, including 46 targets to flip in its "Red To Blue" program, 26 "Frontline" incumbents in potentially tight races and another 19 it considers "Districts In Play."   
   The NRCC has 17 districts on its "Patriots" list of vulnerable incumbents to support and another 27 candidates in open races or challenging Democratic incumbents as part of the "MAGA Majority" program.   
   Not every race will ultimately end up close or see party control change hands. Many of the DCCC's "Districts In Play" gave Trump closer to 60% of the vote in 2024 and have seen little-to-no ad spend from either party.   Then, there are races like Kentucky's 6th Congressional District, where millions of dollars in spending has poured in from both parties — including from Trump-aligned super PACS — in a district Trump won by 15 points.   In Arkansas' 2nd Congressional District, which Trump also won by 15 points, six-figure outside spending targeting Democratic nominee Chris Jones and boosting incumbent Rep. French Hill contributed to the DCCC adding that race to its "Red To Blue" target.    
   According to Ballotpedia tracking, the target lists compiled by the DCCC and NRCC are usually broader in their scope and limited in their success. From 2012-2024, the Democrats won a total of 34% of its target districts and Republicans won 29%.   In some races and places, Republicans and Democrats are beginning to pull back ad reservations for the rest of the year, according to data from ad tracking firm AdImpact, though for different reasons. The most high profile example for Republicans is halting the flow of money in the North Carolina Senate race and redirecting funds to Kansas.   Some House races have seen similar cancellations, too, like the open race in Nebraska's 2nd District that is both a DCCC Red To Blue and NRCC MAGA Majority target.   Still, that data shows close to half a billion dollars in ad reservations have been placed between now and Election Day, showing that in this midterm election neither party is taking anything for granted.   Other races to watch: FL-13, NC-11, OH-10, OH-15

title: Republican congressman tries to outrun a potential blue wave in New York toss-up seat
description: Rep. Mike Lawler, R-NY, speaks during a
body:
Rep. Mike Lawler, R-NY, speaks during a press conference in Chappaqua, New York. Lawler is running in a tight race in a toss-up district that could help determine control of Congress.
                
                    Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images North America
    

   
   ROCKLAND COUNTY, New York – Photos of children and grandchildren line the wall behind the counter at Sparky's Diner, a local joint that sits on the corner of a busy intersection in Garnerville, New York, about an hour outside New York City.   "I've been in this place 50 years, it'll be 51 in February," said Jeannie Nicolakis, the diner's owner. "I started out – I didn't even have my kids at the time – and then I had my kids, and I raised them in here, in a playpen."   But her pride doesn't stop at her family. It extends to her congressman, Mike Lawler, a two-term Republican running for reelection in New York's 17th district. It is one of the closest races in the country in a seat encompassing a string of commuter towns and suburbs around the Hudson River Valley.   
   "He's like my own son. That's how I see him," she said, before adding, "not really my son – because I'm old enough to be his grandmother – but I see him as a grandson that's done so much for this county."   To supporters like Nicolakis, no one can take Lawler's place. But this district is far from a Republican stronghold. It's one of just a handful of places that elected a Republican to the House of Representatives in 2024 and also voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris, a Democrat.   Two years later, Lawler's ability to hold onto the seat could be a deciding factor in determining whether Republicans can keep their narrow majority in the House of Representatives. He faces a competitive challenge from Democrat Cait Conley, a military veteran and former counterterrorism official during the Biden administration who has sought to chip away at the broader coalition that's elected Lawler to congress twice before.   Lawler has tried to position himself as a Republican who is unafraid to cross his own party and highlights examples on the campaign trail, including how he broke with the administration over the decision to end a policy that shielded nearly 350,000 of Haitian migrants from deportation. Lawler says he was able to get the White House to temporarily extend work authorizations for beneficiaries of the program, however that has since expired.   
   He also regularly touts his work to raise the state and local property tax deduction, or SALT cap, a popular issue among his constituents that became a flash point in negotiations over Trump's massive tax and spending bill. Lawler ultimately cast a deciding vote in favor of the legislation, though critics have argued that other key parts of the bill have hurt voters, notably, thesizable cuts to federal healthcare funds.   At the same time, Lawler hasn't shied away from Trump.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rep. Mike Lawler, R-NY, walks on stage on the second day of the Republican National Convention in September.
                
                    Alex Wong/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alex Wong/Getty Images North America
    

   
   "The truth is that the president and I don't always agree, and that's okay. After all, we're both New Yorkers," Lawler said in an address at the Republican National Convention in September. "What I learned about President Trump behind closed doors is that if you're willing to make your case and fight for what you believe in, he's willing to listen."   With less than a month until Election Day, Democrat and Republican-aligned groups have already collectively spent more than $40 million on ad spending in this race.   It comes as national polls show the GOP at a disadvantage, finding that voters are more likely to choose Democrats over Republicans when asked which party's candidate they would back in their district. Plus, President Trump continues to battle historically low approval ratings, with a majority of Americans saying they "strongly disapprove" of his job performance, according to the latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll.   Can voters separate Lawler from his party?   Just outside of Sparky's Diner on a recent sunny Saturday afternoon, a lengthy procession of local first-responders and marching bands participate in the annual Rockland County Volunteer Firefighters Association parade. Lawler walks alongside them, frequently stopping to take selfies and shake hands with residents lining nearby sidewalks.   Despite the national stakes of his race, Lawler remains confident in his victory this fall, asserting that his deep understanding of the district makes him the right person to lead it.   
   "Look, all politics is local," he said in an interview as he neared the end of the parade route.   "My constituents know who I am," he said. "The people who are solely voting on the basis of their dislike of Donald Trump, that's their prerogative, that's their right. But the vast majority of my constituents care about the substance of issues and the policy solutions that we can forge. And I'm proud of the record that I've been able to deliver for this district."   But campaigning as an independent voice within Trump's party may be a tough line for the sitting Republican to walk, especially as voters continue to raise alarm bells about the high cost of living.   Across the Hudson River in the town of Armonk, located within the more liberal-leaning Westchester County, Brett Silverstein is one of many parents trying to keep an eye on their kids as they run around the town's fall festival. He cites high energy prices as a top concern.   "You're paying for goods that are inflated because of how much gasoline is and how much diesel is," he said, adding that while he used to vote for Republicans, he doesn't like Trump and in turn remains doubtful of Lawler's message.   "He's supported Trump and kind of the whole 'MAGA train' over the past 2 to 4 years," he said. "So given how he's affiliated with that, I'm just not a big fan of it in general."   It's an association that's pushed away some of the voters that first backed Lawler in 2022, including self-described moderate Mike Monroe, who ended up casting a ballot against the sitting congressman two years later and plans to again this year.   "He's basically the House of Representatives' version of [Maine Republican Sen.] Susan Collins," said Monroe, who lives in the town of Nanuet, part of Rockland County. "[Lawler] stands up to the Trump administration in certain instances, but only when it doesn't matter."   
   Democrats here walk their own political tight rope   Monroe now volunteers for Conley, who's tried to appeal to Democrats as well as disaffected Republicans and Independents on the campaign trail by arguing that Lawler's record in Congress has made New Yorkers worse off.   "Whether it's somebody who's a registered Republican, Independent or Democrat, [it] doesn't matter," Conley said in an interview. "The pain they're feeling is real for all, regardless of political affiliation."   "It's harder to put food on the table, keep a roof over their heads, afford health care, or keep the lights on. And they deserve better. And I will be better," she added.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Cait Conley, the Democrat running against Rep. Mike Lawler, R-NY, hopes to appeal to Democrats and disaffected Republicans to win in November.
                
                    Spencer Platt/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Spencer Platt/Getty Images North America
    

   
   Conley has also tried to differentiate herself from factions of her party that could turn off swing voters, distancing from high-profile figures on the left like New York City Mayor and democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani. She also hasn't publicly campaigned alongside the state's Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul, who has faced criticism from Lawler and other Republicans in the state particularly over her economic and immigration-related policies.   It's a strategy that could prove helpful for this district where fewer voters are fiercely partisan.   "A lot of swing districts are just swing districts because they're equal number of Democrats and Republicans. That's not really what's going on in NY-17," said Evan Roth Smith, a democratic pollster who runs the firm Slingshot Strategies.   Polling conducted by Slingshot shows that between 30 and 40 percent of voters in the district are either ticket splitters or are only loosely partisan in their personal identification with the parties.   "One cycle they might vote for a Republican, the next cycle they might vote for a Democrat," Roth Smith said. "So it's a swing district because there are a lot of swing voters."   That's the case for retired builder Michael Alvarado, who lives in Stony Point, a town farther north within Rockland.   
   "I vote for whoever thinks my way," he said. "I don't really have a party. I'm not a Republican or a Democrat. Actually I would say I'm more of a Democrat than a Republican."   Though he says he supported Lawler last time, he's still deciding this year, and cares most about backing a candidate who is pro union and will cut school and property taxes.   When asked if anyone is currently speaking to those concerns, Alvarado replies, "not really," but added, he always votes.   "I'm just looking. See what happens come November. We'll hear all the promises."

schema.headline: Republican congressman tries to outrun a potential blue wave in New York toss-up seat

title: Trump proposes Camp David-style presidential retreat at his private Florida golf club
description: FILE - The motorcade for President Donal
body:
FILE - The motorcade for President Donald Trump arrives at Trump International Golf Club, Jan. 2, 2026, in West Palm Beach, Fla.
                
                    Alex Brandon/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alex Brandon/AP
    

   
   FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. — President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he wants to develop one of his Florida golf courses into a presidential retreat where his successors can spend quiet weekends on the greens, describing it as "sort of a Camp David " that he says would already have many of the security features needed to host presidents and world leaders.   
   The proposal for the retreat on Trump's private golf course in West Palm Beach would comingle the presidency with Trump's business ventures beyond his time in office, and is the the latest example of Trump seeking ways to leave his imprint on the presidency.   "It's a great idea, and it'll be used a lot," Trump said, claiming it was suggested by the United States Secret Service. "It seems that all presidents play golf."   The plan has already been submitted to local officials. Trump, an avid golfer, rattled off the benefits of the property a short drive from his Mar-a-Lago home during an unrelated event in the Oval Office, noting that it's close to an airport and has some distance from residential homes and tall buildings, which pose security risks.   
   He did not mention that the golf course was the site of an unsuccessful attempt on his life in 2024. Trump was playing at the Trump International Golf Club during a break from the campaign trail when a Secret Service agent spotted an armed man in the trees lining the club's perimeter fence. The man was arrested after a chase and later convicted of trying to kill Trump, and was sentenced to life in prison.   Past presidents have used Camp David, a rustic compound in Maryland, as a weekend retreat and a place to host presidential meetings. Trump has spent less time there, often opting for his own properties, including golf clubs in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia.   Palm Beach County sees what it calls a 'historic opportunity'   Trump's proposal follows other projects by the lifelong real estate developer to build a White House ballroom, gild the Oval Office, erect a triumphal arch, renovate the Kennedy Center, refurbish the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and rebuild a golf course in East Potomac Park. He has also begun planning a future presidential library in a Miami skyscraper.   In a letter to Palm Beach County commissioners last month, first reported by the Palm Beach Post, an attorney who represents the golf course said Trump is offering to designate it as a "U.S. Presidential Golf Course."   
   "Just as Camp David, Windsor Castle, or the Elysée Palace are known worldwide, so too will the Presidential Golf Course in Palm Beach County," Harvey Oyer said in the letter.   
   Palm Beach County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo said in a statement that local officials are eager to explore what this "historic opportunity" could mean to the community. "This likely would further cement Palm Beach County's place on the national and international stage for generations to come," Abruzzo said.   Oyer's letter said the West Palm Beach golf course could be used by current and former presidents, along with visiting foreign heads of state. The Trump Organization owns the golf club but leases the land from the county, which would need to approve any changes.   Under the proposal, the club would pay to build a new presidential lodging and then work with the Secret Service and other agencies to provide free access to the federal government. The retreat would have a separate entrance from the private club, which earned Trump nearly $37 million during his first year back in office, according to his financial disclosure.   "This is a gift that the President would like to share with his successors, the people of America, and his fellow Palm Beach County residents," Oyer wrote. "It should be noted that President Trump will be out of office before this proposed project could be completed so this is a gift to his successors."   
   Oyer highlighted past U.S. presidents who turned over land for public use. Dwight Eisenhower donated his Gettysburg Farm in Pennsylvania to the National Park Service, and Franklin D. Roosevelt donated part of his estate in Hyde Park, New York.   Years before it was bought by Trump, Mar-a-Lago itself was proposed as a "Winter White House."   Businesswoman and socialite Marjorie Merriweather Post left the home to the National Park Service when she died in 1973, but the agency returned the home to her estate in 1980 because of high maintenance costs. Trump bought the property in 1985, and it later became his primary residence.

title: ICE has quietly used this warehouse as a detention facility all summer, neighbors say
description: A Roxbury, N.J., warehouse was one piece
body:
A Roxbury, N.J., warehouse was one piece of a billion-dollar plan by the Department of Homeland Security to detain migrants.
                
                    José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR
    

   
   ROXBURY, N.J. — On a warm morning on Sept. 4, masked immigration agents rolled into Dover, N.J.   Footage of the raids rippled across social media, sent people into hiding and reignited rumors that had been circulating for months: Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were taking people to a nearby warehouse.   
   The warehouse in Roxbury was one piece of a billion-dollar plan by the Department of Homeland Security to detain migrants as part of President Trump's mass deportation efforts.   That plan to convert warehouses into detention centers faced fierce backlash and legal challenges from residents and immigrant advocates. It was largely abandoned, and in several sites, including Roxbury, the government is legally forbidden by a court order from converting them to a detention facility, pending environmental assessments.   But an NPR investigation has found signs that the New Jersey facility is being used. And the state's Office of the Attorney General says it is looking into similar reports.   
   Contractor says he was told Stephen Miller wanted facilities to be "cruel"   In early 2026, Homeland Security bought 11 warehouses to turn into ICE detention facilities. They spent about a billion dollars on these.   NPR spoke to an official at a government contractor whose company was approached to convert several of the warehouses into ICE facilities. He spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation from the government.   "No one that we spoke to at DHS was for this idea whatsoever. The deputy director told us point-blank that they had pushed back very hard on it. Everybody knew warehouses are horrible places to put people," he says.   
   At a meeting with a deputy director at DHS, he says, his company proposed an alternative: FEMA-style camps in Texas that would be more humane.   He says that idea was swiftly shot down. While White House adviser Stephen Miller was not at the meeting, they were told that this was not what Miller wanted.   The contractor says his understanding from that meeting was that "Miller did not want the facilities that were comfortable. He did not want facilities that were humane. We were told point-blank that that was not what the administration wanted."   
   "Steve Miller certainly seemed to make that point to everyone that he wanted it to be cruel. This was what Miller had stated to the DHS at that time, to the DHS director and deputy director. What surprised me was just how adamant the people were that it was going to happen. Damn the consequences. I would say in 25 years of working with the U.S. government, I've never been in that position before."   In a statement to NPR, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said the contractor's comments were "false hearsay allegation(s) from someone who has never even met or talked with Stephen Miller." Bis also said that Miller "has never made any remarks to anyone about wanting illegal aliens to have worse detention facility conditions. It simply isn't true and this is defamatory."   The White House did not respond to repeated requests to speak to Miller directly.   DHS is holding on to the strategically positioned warehouses   Early on, the warehouse plan was met with protests in both conservative and liberal towns. Several state attorneys general filed lawsuits to halt construction, based on environmental concerns.   "It very quickly became an absolute boondoggle," says Michael Wriston, a former military intelligence analyst who co-founded Project SaltBox, a watchdog group that tracks ICE's expansion. "It was really about the optics of people being kept in these cages and these large warehouses. They wanted a lot of what they called B-roll to play on social media, but they didn't do any due diligence of making sure that they conformed with environmental policy or that the construction wouldn't disturb local water tables."   A DHS official who served during Trump's first term, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared government retaliation, says that while they were not in the meeting the contractor described to NPR, they had often heard higher-ups in the administration wanting to make a point of showcasing difficult conditions immigrants were being held in.    Then, with the departure of DHS Secretary Kristi Noem in March, there was a shift: Her replacement, Secretary Markwayne Mullin, sought to do less showy immigration crackdowns. Today, Homeland Security is selling several of the warehouses.   
   But they're still holding on to a few, including in Hagerstown, Md., Surprise, Ariz., and Roxbury, N.J. "These locations are very critical to ICE's deportation agenda," says Wriston, "because they fill in the gap in places where ICE does not have a robust detention network. They don't have a lot of jails there." They are also located in areas where there are no partnerships with the police who can house detainees in local jails.   In Maryland, Arizona and New Jersey, following lawsuits from each of the state attorneys general, DHS has either agreed or been ordered by a judge to halt the conversion of the warehouses into detention centers, pending environmental impact assessments. But throughout the summer, in the towns surrounding the Roxbury warehouse, rumors started to bubble.   A summer of arrests and rumors   Over the summer, there was a historic surge in ICE arrests: around 100,000 people in July and August.   In New Jersey, the rumor mill started churning. The Roxbury warehouse is located in a wooded area, on a road right off Route 46. Project NINJA (No ICE in North Jersey Alliance), a coalition that opposes ICE detention expansion, says several neighbors reported vehicles, often in a caravan, speeding up the road.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Dover Council Member Sandra Wittner in Dover, N.J., on Sept. 17.
                
                    José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR
    

   
   "They're holding people in that warehouse," one woman says in a WhatsApp group in the town of Dover, which is about 15 minutes from Roxbury. "I have a co-worker who was taken there. They hold them there and at night they take them somewhere else." The message was forwarded to NPR by Dover Council Member Sandra Wittner.   "But, you know, it's like third- and fourth-hand accounts," says Wittner. "It just didn't seem probable at the time because of the court order. But it kind of made you scratch your head a little bit."   Then the morning of Sept. 4 happened.   
   "We were taken to the Roxbury warehouse"   A woman says she was driving to work when she saw a raid taking place in Dover. She decided to follow the car carrying people who were detained. "I just needed to know, is he going to Roxbury?"    She took video as she trailed them up Route 46. She asked that NPR not use her name because what happened next made her fearful of what the government might do.   She says the car she was following turned onto the woodsy road that leads to the warehouse.   
   She says she waited to see if there was any more movement.   "And then maybe five minutes after that, a white Dodge Durango started kind of circling around me," she says. "And then on his last loop, he started filming me. He had a yellow case on his cellphone. After that, a black Tahoe started doing the same thing. I was on a public sidewalk, and it was intimidating. It was really intimidating. I'm scared. But I am more scared for our community."   Councilwoman Wittner says she strongly suspects ICE is using the Roxbury warehouse: "The immigration enforcement activity happened in Dover between 7 a.m. and 8 a.m." Wittner points to the woman who was able to follow the vehicle up Route 46: "The last vehicle entered the warehouse road at 8:25 a.m."   Meanwhile, footage of the raid started circulating on social media.   Back in Dover, another woman says she saw the videos as she got her kids ready for school. NPR viewed the videos and confirmed their authenticity.   In one of them, a worker is cornered against a wall by two masked agents. She says she was thunderstruck.   "That's my father," she told NPR.   She asked that we not use her name because she fears being targeted.   At 8:25 a.m., she says, she got a call from her father. He's 59, she says, and he sounded disoriented. He told her he was handcuffed in some kind of jail.   
   She found it strange, she says, because the Roxbury warehouse would be the only place he could have been taken in that short a time span.   She also discovered a friend of hers had been picked up.   
   She hasn't been able to speak to her father since then, and neither has NPR. But NPR located her friend in Honduras, where he's been deported. He requested anonymity, because he fears repercussions for his loved ones who are still in the U.S.   "I was picked up on my way to work, on Friday, Sept. 4. The agents loaded me into a van. They took us to Roxbury," he said.   He says he and the other people detained were handcuffed and held in the parking lot for several hours. He counted nine other men with him. "I just went into a state of shock," he says. "I signed my deportation papers. The next morning I regretted it. But I was scared. Eventually, they transferred us to a real facility."   In a statement to NPR, DHS did not respond to a question about whether it was holding people at the Roxbury location. But it did give NPR a statement it has previously sent about ICE detention, saying DHS upholds strict standards and that immigrants can choose to leave detention by being deported.   "We need our Congress members to conduct an oversight visit yesterday"   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A member of Project NINJA, a coalition that opposes ICE detention expansion, in Roxbury on Sept. 17.
                
                    José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR
    

   
   The activists at NINJA say ICE's actions violate the legal order. The order lists several actions ICE can take with the site — mainly upkeep — but nowhere on that list is detention an acceptable action, they say.   Harvard professor Andrew Mergen, a former attorney with the U.S. Department of Justice Environment & Natural Resources Division, says ICE may technically not be violating the court order, which stipulated it would not convert the place into a detention center pending an environmental assessment.   
   Ultimately, Mergen says, the situation shows the limitations of using environmental claims. "The community is acting here to prevent people from being detained," says Mergen. "And the administration seems to have cleverly elided that intention, by sort of saying, 'Well, we're not going to build this facility, but we're going to use this space in furtherance of detention.'"   He says he understands the frustration: "It's just infuriating if what you are trying to do is say 'No. Not here. Not here.' "   
   Wittner says since the raid, she's heard from other close relatives or close friends of two men who were picked up that day, who say they were inside the Roxbury warehouse.   She says the situation is unacceptable: "We need our Congress members to conduct an oversight visit yesterday, quite honestly. We need our state to aggressively pursue this investigation and demand to get inside."   She says DHS has had time "to go in and clean up their mess if they, in fact, got caught doing something that they shouldn't have."   Meanwhile, in Dover, the streets where the raid happened remain deserted.   At an empty diner at lunchtime, a waitress who did not want to be named because of the climate of fear in town says one of the workers who was taken used to come here for a bite.   Then she leans over and asks: "Do you know where they took those men?"   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The warehouse in Roxbury.
                
                    José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR

schema.headline: ICE has quietly used this warehouse as a detention facility all summer, neighbors say
